en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek leaves the subject of this half unstated.

01.r: Adds the next step of the argument.

02.r: In the one case: the Levitical priests.
02.n: The BSB writes 'In the case of the Levites', which names who 'here' means. That is a fair reading of the chapter, but the word itself is only 'here'.
t: In the case of the Levites

03.r: Sets up the contrast completed by 'but' in the second half.
03.n: Abbott-Smith calls this particle 'generally untranslatable'. It pairs with δέ later in the verse: here on the one hand, there on the other. Most translations leave it out.

04.r: The tenth part paid to the priests.
04.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses this word for Hebrew מַעֲשֵׂר, the tithe, including at Genesis 14:20, where Abram gives the tenth to Melchizedek.

05.r: Men subject to death, set against the one who lives.
05.n: A present participle: literally 'dying men', men who are in the process of dying. The BSB's 'mortal' captures the contrast with 'he lives'.

07.r: The priests take in the tithe.
07.n: This is the same verb as 'having received' in Matthew 25:24 on this page. The BSB's 'collect' leans toward taxation language.

08.n: The Greek has no verb in this half. The KJV and Geneva supply 'he receiveth them', and the BSB names Melchizedek outright.

09.r: Completes the contrast opened by μέν.

10.n: The participle is passive: he is the one testified about. The writer does not say who testifies. The likeliest reading is the Scripture account of Melchizedek, but that is an inference.

11.r: Introduces the content of the testimony.

12.r: Present tense: he goes on living, set against the dying men.
12.n: The YLT's 'he was living' departs from the present tense of the Greek. The BSB's 'lives on' brings out the continuing sense.
